content:
Start by treating $k$ as a fixed number and writing the system as a matrix equation:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 1 & k \\
1 & k & 1 \\
k & 1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
x \\
y \\
z
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 \\
1 \\
1
\end{bmatrix}
$$

The coefficient matrix is the square matrix multiplying the unknowns. Its determinant tells you whether the system has a unique solution: if the determinant is nonzero, the matrix is invertible, so there is exactly one solution.

If the determinant is zero, that test alone can’t tell you whether there are infinitely many solutions or none. Then you check whether the equations are consistent—for example, by row-reducing the coefficient matrix together with the right-hand side.

Your next step: calculate the determinant of the coefficient matrix as an expression in $k$.

content:
Exercise 4 says: “For which values of $k$ does the system $x+y+kz=1,\ x+ky+z=1,\ kx+y+z=1$ have unique, infinite or no solutions?”

Your first two cofactor terms are correct. In the third term, the minor is $1-k^2$, so that contribution is $k(1-k^2)$, not $k(k^2-1)$. The sign changes because the minor is $1\cdot1-k\cdot k$.

Thus the corrected determinant is

$$
(k-1)-(1-k)+k(1-k^2)=-k^3+3k-2.
$$

Factor this expression to find the values of $k$ where the determinant is zero.

content:
Exercise 4 says: “For which values of $k$ does the system $x+y+kz=1,\ x+ky+z=1,\ kx+y+z=1$ have unique, infinite or no solutions?”

For this exercise, the coefficient matrix is

$$
A=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 1 & k \\
1 & k & 1 \\
k & 1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

A nonzero determinant means the rows and columns of $A$ are independent. For a square matrix, that makes $A$ invertible, so the system $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ has exactly one solution for any right-hand side $\mathbf{b}$.

A square matrix has determinant zero exactly when it is **singular**. That is equivalent to its columns being dependent, which means there is a nonzero vector $\mathbf{h}$ such that $A\mathbf{h}=\mathbf{0}$. If $\mathbf{x}_0$ is one solution, then

$$
A(\mathbf{x}_0+t\mathbf{h})
=
A\mathbf{x}_0+tA\mathbf{h}
=
\mathbf{b}
$$

for every real number $t$. Since $\mathbf{h}\ne\mathbf{0}$, distinct values of $t$ give distinct solutions. So if a solution exists, there are infinitely many; if none exists, the system is inconsistent and has no solutions. The determinant alone cannot distinguish those two cases.

First find the values of $k$ that make the determinant zero. Then, for each such value, row-reduce the augmented matrix and check whether the system is consistent.

issues.where: “A nonzero determinant means the rows and columns of $A$ are independent.”
issues.fix: Explain that the determinant is zero exactly when the square matrix is singular, equivalently when its columns are dependent and there is a nonzero vector $\mathbf{h}$ with $A\mathbf{h}=\mathbf{0}$. This connects the determinant test to the later argument.

Clarify that if $\mathbf{x}_0$ is a solution and $\mathbf{h}\ne\mathbf{0}$ is in the nullspace, then every real $t$ gives a solution, and distinct $t$ give distinct solutions. This makes the claim of infinitely many solutions clear.
